blocks.content: Introduction to Antennas & RF safety basics
Recognize antenna inspection and RF safety precautions.

items.definition: Regular VHF antenna inspection: (1) physical condition — no cracks, chips, or broken base; (2) secure mounting — no looseness; (3) connector tightness — coax connector properly torqued; (4) coaxial cable condition — no kinks, chafing, or water infiltration; (5) no corrosion at base or connector.
items.analogy: Like inspecting a car antenna — check the element, the base mounting, and the cable all the way to where it connects to the radio.

items.definition: Radio frequency (RF) radiation from transmitting antennas can cause tissue heating, eye damage, and interference with medical devices at close range. ALWAYS de-energize the transmitter before working on or near the antenna. This applies to all RF systems: VHF comm, transponder, DME, ADS-B.
items.analogy: Like not looking directly into a laser — the energy is invisible but can cause real harm at close range.

items.definition: When replacing coax for a VHF antenna: (1) use correct impedance cable (50Ω for VHF comm), (2) use correct cable type/spec for the run length and environment, (3) install connectors properly — correct preparation, crimping, and torque, (4) measure SWR (Standing Wave Ratio) to verify the installation.
items.analogy: Like replacing a garden hose — use the right diameter (impedance), connect fittings properly (connectors), then check for leaks (SWR).

items.definition: Three most common causes of intermittent or noisy comm audio: (1) loose or corroded connector (high contact resistance causing noise), (2) damaged coaxial cable (bent, kinked, or crushed center conductor), (3) failing microphone jack (worn or oxidized contacts causing noise when moving).
items.analogy: Like a lamp that flickers — most often it's a loose bulb, damaged cord, or worn socket, not the lamp itself.

blocks.question: What should be checked during a regular VHF communication antenna inspection?
choices: Antenna impedance using a network analyzer and SWR meter
The antenna radiation pattern using a calibrated antenna range
The radio's transmitted power output and frequency accuracy
Physical condition, mounting security, connector tightness, coax condition, and corrosion
blocks.feedback: A standard VHF antenna inspection is visual and physical: check for physical damage to the element, verify it's securely mounted with no wobble, confirm the coax connector is tight, inspect the coax for damage, and check for corrosion at all contact points. An SWR measurement can be added after any maintenance.

blocks.question: What is the key safety requirement when performing maintenance near an aircraft VHF antenna?
choices: Ensure the RF transmitting system is off before working near the antenna
Keep the system in low-power standby mode to reduce risk
Wear RF-shielded gloves rated for VHF frequencies
Only approach the antenna from behind to avoid the main radiation lobe
blocks.feedback: The only safe approach is to de-energize the system. RF can cause tissue injury at close range — 'standby' or 'low power' modes still transmit and are not safe for nearby work. Always verify the system is off before working at the antenna or along the transmission line.

blocks.question: What are the critical steps when replacing coaxial cable on a VHF communication antenna?
choices: Only match cable length to the original; impedance doesn't matter for short runs
Replace the antenna at the same time for guaranteed performance
Use correct impedance and cable type, install and torque connectors properly, verify SWR after installation
Only SWR verification is required — cable type and connector torque are secondary
blocks.feedback: All three steps are critical: wrong impedance creates a mismatch (increased reflected power, reduced range); improperly installed connectors cause intermittent connection and RF leakage; without SWR verification, a hidden fault may not be detected until the radio fails in flight.

blocks.question: What are the most common causes of intermittent or noisy audio in an aircraft communication system?
choices: Incorrectly programmed squelch threshold and volume setting
Software version mismatch between the radio and audio panel
Loose or corroded connectors, damaged coaxial cable, or failing microphone jack
Alternator noise from an unfiltered electrical bus
blocks.feedback: The vast majority of intermittent/noisy comm audio issues are physical connection problems: corroded or loose connectors create variable resistance; damaged coax (kinked, crushed, water-infiltrated) degrades signal; failing mic jacks introduce noise with movement. These should be the first inspection points.
